title: The workers hired late (Matthew 20:1–16)
hookLine: those who worked one hour get the same wage as those who worked all day

cards: Dawn in the town square. Men are standing around, waiting to be picked for a day's work, the way day laborers still wait outside hardware stores this morning.
A landowner comes and hires some for his vineyard, for a denarius a day; the Douay-Rheims calls it a penny. Mid-morning he comes back and hires more. At noon, more.
Mid-afternoon, more. And at the eleventh hour, with the day nearly gone, he finds men still standing there. "Why stand you here all the day idle?"
Because no one hired us, they say. Go on, then, he says, into the vineyard. Then evening comes, and it's time to pay.

teach.b: The landowner tells his steward: pay them, starting with the last ones hired. The eleventh-hour crew steps up and gets a full denarius.

teach.h: A FULL DAY'S WAGE FOR ONE HOUR.
teach.b: A whole day's wage for one hour. Down the line, the dawn crew starts counting: if they got a denarius, we're getting a lot more. Then they get a denarius, exactly what they agreed to.
And they grumble. These last worked one hour, and you've made them equal to us, who bore the burden of the day and the heat. Their complaint sounds fair.
He answers one of them: friend, I'm doing you no wrong. Didn't you agree to a denarius? Take what's yours and go.
In the Douay-Rheims: "Or, is it not lawful for me to do what I will? is thy eye evil, because I am good?" Some readers hear envy in that phrase: a look that resents someone else's good luck.
The dawn workers weren't cheated. The problem is that someone else was given a gift. "So shall the last be first, and the first last."
The Catholic Church teaches that grace is like this: a free gift, undeserved, not wages earned.
The Catechism describes it as favor: help from God that is free and undeserved. Nobody clocks in for it.

This whole week's stories say it: a sower throwing seed everywhere, a seed and some yeast, a Samaritan stopping, a sheep and a coin found, two sons and a father who runs, and now a payday that makes no sense on a spreadsheet.

how: Catholics hear this parable at Sunday Mass, and the Catechism teaches that grace is a free and undeserved gift from God; some use the story to examine envy before confession.

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.
p: the agreed wage for a day
one hour, a full day's pay

s: the dawn workers were paid less than they agreed to
they got exactly the denarius they agreed to. someone else got a gift.
the landowner pays the last ones hired first
so the dawn crew watches the eleventh-hour crew get a full day's wage.
the landowner says he did the dawn workers no wrong
they agreed to a denarius, and they got it.

games.q: you worked from dawn. you just watched men who worked one hour get a full day's wage. you get the same. what does the landowner say when you complain?
o: I did you no wrong. are you envious because I am good?
next time I'll pay by the hour.
games.why: “is it not lawful for me to do what I will? is thy eye evil, because I am good?” the last shall be first, and the first last.

practice: Think of someone who recently got something good: a raise, a baby, a trip, praise you felt you deserved more.
If there's a little sting, don't scold yourself; just picture their face when they got the good news, and for one breath, try to be glad with them. If you pray, you can thank God for their gift.

wordCard.voice: denarius. The day's wage every worker agreed to, whether hired at dawn or with the day nearly gone.

orig.note: Greek, from Latin denarius: a silver coin; in the parable, the agreed wage for a day.

carryVoice: Your line: grace isn't a wage. Day forty-nine, and next week, signs on the road.
